blocks.text: The word נכאת necoth, of very uncertain meaning, in Genes. XXXVII, 25. and XLIII, 11., is explained by Jonathan as שעוא and by Erpenianus as شمعا [shamʿan], that is, wax, as also by the author of Beresith Rabba, section 91, near the end. And in Onkelos they think that שעך is the very same thing, because it comes close to שעוא. However that may be, other interpreters explain it very differently. The LXX have θυμίαμα [thymiama] or θυμιάματα [thymiamata]; Aquila, στύρακα [styraka]; Jerome in the first passage aromata [spices], in the second storacem [storax], like Aquila; the Syriac ܪ̈ܗܛܢܐ, resin; the Samaritan ࠒࠈࠐ, balsam; the Arabic version published at Paris, خرنوبا [kharnūban], just as some in Kimchi have חרוב, carob; two Arabic manuscripts in Sweden صمغا [ṣamghan], gum; Rabbi Moses the Priest and Kimchi, דבר נחמד, a desirable thing; R. Selomo, כנוסי בשמים הרבה, collections of many spices. In this doubtful matter the later writers follow one or another of the older ones, as seemed good to them. Junius alone, taking a path of his own, rendered it myxaria [sebesten plums], which, he says, are called in Arabic NUKETA, according to Aegineta, Aëtius, Psellus and Actuarius, a word very close to the Hebrew NEKOTH. But this man, otherwise pious and learned, has missed the point. For the Arabic name of the sebesten, مخيط [mukhayṭ] mucchait, as the Arabs consistently write it, has not a single letter in common with the Hebrew נכאת nechoth, as anyone who is not entirely ἀναλφάβητος [analphabētos] in these languages will at once recognize. Nor do the authors he cites mention the Arabic name; among the Greeks only Charito, as far as I know, does so, writing μουχαῖτας [mouchaitas], as the apothecaries write mukeitas and mokaitas. Most of the other more recent writers explain נכאת necoth as θυμιάματα [thymiamata], spices, with the Greeks, Jerome and some of the Hebrews. That this can hardly stand will be evident to anyone who reads the two passages of Scripture in which this word occurs. The first reads thus, Gen. XXXVII, 25. Lifting up their eyes they saw; and behold, a company of Ishmaelite travellers coming from Gilead, whose camels were carrying נכאת nechoth, and resin, and stacte; and they were going to carry them down into Egypt. And the second, Gen. XLIII, 11. Take of the most praised fruits of this land in your vessels, to carry a gift to that man, a little resin, נכאת nechoth, and stacte, and pistachios, and almonds. From reading these the attentive reader will see that נכאת is not θυμιάματα [thymiamata], or spices, or a desirable thing [III, 400] in general, but something particular, like honey, resin, stacte, etc., which are mentioned in the same place. And I have several reasons why Aquila, who rendered it storax, pleases me most. Let the first be this: that storax grows abundantly in Syria. Pliny, book 12, chapter 25: Syria, next to Judaea, above Phoenicia, produces storax around Gabala and Marathus, and Casius, the mountain of Seleucia. Dioscorides, book 2, after giving the marks of the best storax, says Τοιοῦτος δέ ἐστιν ὁ Καταβαλίτης, καὶ Πισσιδιακὸς, καὶ Κιλίκιος [Toioutos de estin ho Katabalitēs, kai Pissidiakos, kai Kilikios], where for ὁ Καταβαλίτης [ho Katabalitēs] one should read ὁ Γαβαλίτης [ho Gabalitēs], that is, from the very well-known city of Syria, Gabala, which Pliny mentions. Others assign it to Phoenicia, like Artemidorus in Stephanus under Κάρνη [Karnē]. And Josephus to Galilee, Antiquities book 15, chapter 23. Second, storax is rightly counted among the most praised fruits of the land, since physicians particularly commend its use among the spices. Third, as here the Ishmaelites, so in Pliny, book 12, chapter 17, the Arabs bring back storax from Syria. Fourth, it is not without reason that Moses joins storax with resin, [col. 533] honey and stacte of myrrh, since it approaches their nature. Accordingly Dioscorides describes the best storax as ῥητινώδης [rhētinōdēs], resinous, καὶ ἐν τῷ μαλάσσεσθαι ἀνεὶς ὑγρασίαν τινὰ μελιτώδη [kai en tō malassesthai aneis hygrasian tina melitōdē], and when kneaded giving off a honey-like liquid. And to it is attributed δάκρυον κόμμι ἐοικὸς, διαυγὲς, σμηρνίζον [dakryon kommi eoikos, diauges, smērnizon], a tear like gum, translucent, like myrrh. So also Isidore, book 17, chapter 8: Storax calamites, fat, resinous, of a pleasant smell, moist, and as it were giving off a honeyed liquid. Hence in Pliny storax is adulterated with cedar resin, or gum, at other times with honey. Fifth, I think I can detect the origin of the Hebrew name, hitherto unknown. The Arabic verb نكت [nakata] nachatha means 1. to strike the ground with a spear so that a mark remains impressed; 2. to throw someone pierced by a spear on his head; and النكت [al-nakt] is such a piercing, and النكات [al-nakkāt] one who pierces thus. Why should the Hebrew name of storax, נכאת nechoth, not allude to this, since from the storax tree are made τὰ στυράκινα ἀκοντίσματα ἐοικότα τοῖς κρανεΐνοις [ta styrakina akontismata eoikota tois kraneinois], storax javelins similar to those made of cornel? So it is in Strabo, book 12. And accordingly in the Greek Hesychius σύραξ [syrax] means not only storax, the tree or the spice, but also a lance, and a part of the spear, either the lowest or the highest. For the ancients do not agree well on this. In Pollux, book 1, chapter 10: Τὸ μὲν τέλος τοῦ δόρατος σαυρωτὴρ, τὸ δὲ προῦχον αἰχμὴ, καὶ ἐπιδορατὶς, καὶ στύραξ [To men telos tou doratos saurōtēr, to de prouchon aichmē, kai epidoratis, kai styrax], the lowest part of the spear is the sauroter, and the top the point, and the styrax. Yet in the same author, book 10, chapter 31, σαυρωτὴρ [saurōtēr] and στύραξ [styrax] are the same. So also in Hesychius, Suidas and the Etymologicum. And in Athenaeus, book 12, Heraclides of Cyme describes the μηλοφόροι [mēlophoroi] of the Persians, the melophori, ἐπὶ τῶν συράκων μῆλα χρυσᾶ ἔχοντες [epi tōn syrakōn mēla chrysa echontes], having golden apples on their styraces (that is, on the tops of their spear-shafts). And this is precisely the στυράκιον [styrakion] in book 2 of Thucydides, where we read that a certain Plataean shut the gates of the city στυρακίῳ ἀντὶ [styrakiō anti] [III, 401] βαλάνου χρησάμενος ἐς τὸν μοχλὸν [balanou chrēsamenos es ton mochlon], driving the butt of a spear-shaft into the bar instead of a bolt-pin. And the verb συρακίζειν [syrakizein] in Hesychius is κεντρίζειν [kentrizein], to prick, as with a spear or the point of a spear. Sixth, if we contend by authority, Aquila, for whom נכאת nechoth is σύραξ [syrax], is followed by Jerome at Gen. XLIII, 11., where he renders storax. And in the Book of Names you may read NECHOTA, storax, or spices. I suspect that the Syrians, who explained it as resin, and the Arabs, who explained it as gum, held the same view, but misused a generic name because the specific one was unknown to them. With נכאת nechoth, the spice, the Hebrews wrongly confuse נכותה necotha, which is plainly something else, Es. XXXIX, 2. and 2 Reg. XX, 13., as will be said elsewhere ^{(12)}.
